title: The 7-Day Restart Plan
subtitle: One week of ten-minute movements to prove to yourself you can start

about.checked: The checking was done with AI. In October 2026 each source on the next pages was opened and read, and this guide was compared with it. A second, separate check then opened every one again. Between them the two checks led to 6 corrections, all made in this version.
changes: The stop-and-rest advice now says when to ring 999 (911 in the US).
The strength figure is corrected: about one in six over-65s in England does enough.

blocks.h1: Welcome — and well done for opening this

blocks.lead: Most people who mean to get more active never begin, because the first step looks too big. This plan makes it small: seven days, ten minutes each, nothing to buy, nothing to be good at. At the end you will know something about yourself that you cannot know today.

blocks.p: You do not need to be fit, thin, sporty or brave. You need a sturdy chair, a worktop or wall to hold, comfortable shoes and ten minutes. If you have knees that grumble or a back that stiffens, that is normal and you are exactly who this is for.

callout.title: Before you start
callout.text:
If you have a heart condition, uncontrolled blood pressure, have fainted or had chest pain in the last year, have had a fall in the last six months or have been told to avoid exercise, have a quick word with your GP or practice nurse first. This is a gentle programme and most will be pleased.
Stop and rest if you feel chest pain or tightness, sudden breathlessness, faintness, or sharp pain in a joint. Call 999 (911 in the US) if chest pain does not go away, spreads to an arm, the neck, jaw or back, or comes with sweating or feeling sick, if you cannot get your breath, or if you faint. Ordinary next-day muscle ache is fine; it means you did something.
This is general information, not medical advice.

blocks.h2: Day 0 — two numbers to write down

numbers: **Sit-to-stand.** From a firm chair, arms crossed if you can, stand fully and sit fully as many times as you comfortably can in 30 seconds. Count them. Using your hands is allowed; note it, and do it the same way on the same chair on Day 7.
**How do you feel today?** Score yourself 1 to 10, where 1 is stiff, tired and unsteady and 10 is loose and sure-footed. First instinct.

rows: Seated. Point toes away, then pull them up towards you. Slow and full.
Seated, tall. Lift one knee a little, lower, then the other.
Seated. Straighten one knee until the leg is level, hold a breath, lower slowly.
Roll shoulders up, back and down in a slow circle.
Feet flat, slightly back. Lean forward, stand, lower slowly. Hands if needed.
Standing, holding support. Rise onto the toes, pause, lower slowly.
Standing, holding support. Lift one leg out to the side without leaning. Lower with control.
Standing, holding support, chair behind you. Bend knees part way as if to sit, stand back up.
Hands on wall at shoulder height, feet a stride back. Chest towards wall, push away.
Hand on support. Lift one foot a little and hold, looking at a fixed point.
Standing, hand near support. Lift knees alternately.
Indoors or out, at a pace where you could still talk.

days.task: Ankle pumps ×10 each, shoulder rolls ×8, seated march ×20, knee extension ×8 each, sit-to-stand ×3 (10 min)
days.note: Slow counts. Today is about turning up.

days.task: Seated march ×20, knee extension ×8 each, sit-to-stand ×4, heel raises at the chair ×8, shoulder rolls ×8 (10 min)
days.note: Lower into the chair slowly — the way down is work too.

days.task: Sit-to-stand ×5, heel raises ×10, side leg raise ×6 each, marching on the spot 1 min, single-leg stand 5 sec each with hand on (10 min)
days.note: Both hands on the worktop. Nothing to prove.

days.task: Mini squat ×6, wall push-up ×8, heel raises ×10, seated march ×20, sit-to-stand ×5 (10 min)
days.note: Mini squat: weight in the heels, chest up.

days.task: Marching on the spot 1 min, indoor or outdoor walk 4 min, side leg raise ×8 each, sit-to-stand ×6 (10 min)
days.note: A pace where you can still talk, but not sing.

days.task: Sit-to-stand ×6, mini squat ×8, wall push-up ×10, single-leg stand 8 sec each, heel raises ×12 (10 min)
days.note: Try the single-leg stand with two fingertips instead of a full hand.

days.task: Retest: sit-to-stands in 30 seconds, and your 1–10 score. Then a 6-minute walk somewhere you like (10 min)
days.note: Write the Day 7 numbers in the table. Compare.

blocks.p: Do the two-minute version and still tick the box: sit-to-stand ×3, heel raises ×10, march for 30 seconds, one slow breath. The habit matters more than any single day.

Many people manage a few more sit-to-stands after a week — mostly practice and confidence at this stage. The feel-score often moves more. If neither moves, that is fine. Neither number is the point. The point is that you did seven days, which most people never do, and you now know the ten minutes fits in your life.

bullets: **Keep going with The 30-Day Restart** (£5 at dontdieretired.com/shop). It picks up exactly here: four weeks from chair to standing to walking to stairs, with a self-test at each end and a two-minute fallback for bad days.

**Already steady on your feet?** Go straight to **Strong at 60**, our 12-week beginner strength plan for home or gym — the twice-a-week strength work that the UK Chief Medical Officers recommend and fewer than one in five over-65s in England actually do.

**Read a story a day.** Every morning at dontdieretired.com we publish a real, sourced story of someone over 50 who started something — a marathon at 70, a doctorate at 80, a surfboard at 60 — with one small thing you can try.

quote.text: You do not have to be good at this. You just have to turn up for ten minutes, and then turn up again tomorrow.

sources.publisher: UK Chief Medical Officers (Department of Health and Social Care)
sources.title: UK Chief Medical Officers' physical activity guidelines
sources.supports: The official UK advice: some activity is better than none, no minimum session length, and strength and balance work on two days a week.

sources.title: Physical activity guidelines for older adults
sources.supports: Speak to a GP first if you have a medical condition, and how to judge your pace: you can still talk, but not sing.

sources.publisher: NHS England, Health Survey for England
sources.title: Health Survey for England, 2021 part 2: Adult physical activity
sources.supports: How few people do strength work: in England in 2021, 17 per cent of adults aged 65 and over met the muscle-strengthening guideline.

sources.publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), STEADI programme
sources.title: 30-Second Chair Stand
sources.supports: The Day 0 and Day 7 test is a standard check of leg strength; the official version uses no hands.

sources.title: Strength exercises
sources.supports: The NHS's own home routine, with pictures: sit-to-stand, mini-squats, calf raises, sideways leg lifts and wall press-ups, at least twice a week.
